normalized.governing_thought: Fix gross margin and delivery economics rather than cutting labor: four quick moves protect the FY2026 covenant, and the full plan restores 3.0% by FY2028
executive_summary: The decline is mainly in gross margin and e-commerce, not wages. Operating margin fell 2.35 pts (3.37% → 1.02%). Gross margin lost 1.02 pts (promotions −0.70, shrink −0.50, private label +0.18) and e-commerce fulfillment 0.84 pts. Store labor cost only 0.30 pts, because 6% higher productivity absorbed most of the 9.4% wage rise.

Management's 8% labor cut would not reach the target. It saves $14.6M, but thinner staffing is linked to higher shrink worth an estimated $5–10M. FY2026 operating income would land at $19–24M against the $20M covenant, and FY2028 margin at only 0.9–1.2%.

A margin-led plan restores ~3.0% for ~$20M of one-time cost. Six levers backed by Harlow's own data (promotions, shrink, labor rebalancing, six lease lapses, private label, delivery fees) take operating income to ~$36M (2.5%) after the 2027 wage step. Three negotiated levers (vendor funding, three lease exits, the delivery contract) add ~$6M, for ~$42M, or 3.0%.

Act first on what is fast, cheap and proven, and hold contingencies. In the first 90 days: roll out the tested delivery fee, cancel money-losing promotions, protect fresh and receiving hours, and reject the 3% delivery-rate rise. FY2026 then reaches ~$24M (about $4M above the covenant). 3.0% has no cushion, so contingency levers are pre-agreed.
Decisions requested today: adopt this plan in place of the 8% labor cut; approve up to $20.5M of one-time spend; schedule a vote on exiting three long-lease stores.

slides.title: We started with a 'margin, not wages' hypothesis. The evidence supports the diagnosis, but commercial fixes alone reach only ~1.8%, so the answer had to grow

claims.claim: Labor is a minor cause of the decline: Supported
evidence: Labor explains 0.30 of the 2.35-pt fall (13%). Wage +9.4%, hours per $1,000 of sales −6%

claims.claim: Gross-margin erosion comes from drivers Harlow controls: Supported
evidence: Promo mix (−0.70), shrink (−0.50) and private label (+0.18) add up to the full −1.02 pts

claims.claim: The extra promotions are not paying back: Supported, but the response to ValuMart is uncertain
evidence: 38% of events lose money; vendor funding fell 55% → 46%; the 'more expensive' score rose 33% → 41%

claims.claim: E-commerce loses money and repricing fixes it: Partly: repricing helps but does not fix it
evidence: It loses ~$10.4M on an incremental basis. The fee test recovers ~$2.5M, but delivery still loses $9 per order

claims.claim: Gross-margin and e-commerce fixes alone reach 3%: Not supported
evidence: Promo, shrink, private label and fees add ~$18.8M, but the wage step and delivery rate (−$7.6M) leave ~$26.5M, or 1.8%

claims.claim: Revised answer: keep the gross-margin and e-commerce core, and add two levers the first hypothesis left out: (a) targeted labor productivity to absorb the 2027 wage step, rather than an 8% cut, and (b) exits from the weakest stores, starting with the six whose leases lapse by 2027. Vendor funding and the delivery contract close the last gap.

slides.title: Gross margin and e-commerce explain 80% of the 2.35-point fall in operating margin; store labor explains only 13%

Labor (−0.30 pts, 13%): labor is the largest cost increase in dollars, but most of that just tracked sales
One more year like FY2025 would take margin to about −0.2%, an operating loss, against a $20M covenant

normalized.recommendation: Adopt the margin-led plan and a FY2028 target of at least 3.0% in place of the 8% labor-hour cut, keeping the freeze for home delivery only; approve up to $20.5M of one-time spend over FY2026–FY2028 with the remaining $4.5M held in reserve and released by the board; ask management to bring the case for the three long-lease stores to the Q3 FY2026 meeting (non-renewal of the six expiring leases is the default).

Not chosen: the three long-lease stores have the weakest payback (3.4–4.1 years) and need a board vote; waiting two quarters costs ~$1.1M and avoids paying $7.5M to exit stores that might turn around.

assumptions_and_uncertainties: All FY2028 figures are run-rate on the FY2025 sales base; no like-for-like sales growth and no inflation other than the known 2027 wage step.
3.0% has no cushion: each key risk would cost about 0.2–0.3 points; combined downside 2.32% ($32M).
Response of ValuMart / volume loss to fewer promotions is uncertain; 15% of shifted promo volume lost assumed, valued at 20% contribution.
The 14-pt gap is read as net of vendor funding (drives ~$90M vendor-pool estimate).
Shrink time-series link to hours is a correlation, used as a risk range, not a forecast; equal sales weight per quartile assumed.
30% of online sales are new to Harlow (survey); fee test (4 stores, 10 weeks) assumed to scale chain-wide; lost sales lost at 20% contribution.
Wage step +4% applied to whole store labor bill (conservative).
Six and three stores are pro-rata shares of the nine-store totals; store-level data should confirm before each lease decision; 25% sales transfer at 12%.
Closure running costs (~$0.5M per store) and all one-time costs except the $7.5M lease exit are team estimates, to be confirmed by Finance.
Fiscal timing: FY2026 treated as first plan year; if FY2026 already closed by February 2027, Year 1 shifts to FY2027.
FY2026 bridge assumes the FY2023–25 drift stops once the actions start; in-year capture rates assumed.
How customers react to the labor changes is untested; occupancy and SG&A may keep rising faster than sales.
Sales risk of service cuts in management plan untested and not included.
All choices were made without access to management; each should be confirmed before the board meeting.
next_steps: Wave 1 (first 90 days): roll out $7.99 fee / $100 free-delivery threshold; cancel failing promotions (no funding, no feature); stop the 8% cut and ring-fence fresh and receiving hours; reject the 3% delivery rate rise and tender the contract.
Wave 2 (FY2026 H2 – FY2027): do not renew the six expiring leases; demand-based scheduling in Q3–Q4 stores; fresh-waste and receiving program; private-label range expansion and vendor-funding round.
Wave 3 (FY2027 – FY2028): board vote and exit of three long-lease stores.
Bring the case for the three long-lease stores to the Q3 FY2026 board meeting.
Track five quarterly KPIs: promo share, vendor funding, shrink, net e-commerce fulfillment cost, operating income.
Change management measures: category team on promotion profit; e-commerce on incremental contribution including delivery; store operations on shrink as well as labor hours.
Finance to confirm one-time cost estimates before the board meeting; confirm assumptions and store-level data before each lease decision.
